tagline.text: A vast reservoir where an old town's church ruins rise from the water in droughts

location.label: Location
location.text: Around Pantabangan Dam, Pantabangan, Nueva Ecija

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: March–May dry season (old town ruins may surface when the water is low)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱800–2,000 (transport, boat and meals, rough estimate for a day trip from Manila)

children.text: Pantabangan Lake is a huge reservoir created by Pantabangan Dam in Nueva Ecija, and the roughly 300-year-old town of Old Pantabangan lies beneath its waters. When a drought drops the water level sharply, the church cross, the cemetery and the plaza site rise above the surface and can be visited by boat.
Pantabangan Lake is an artificial lake in the municipality of Pantabangan, Nueva Ecija. It is the reservoir behind Pantabangan Dam on the Pampanga River; at full level its surface covers about
and it holds roughly 3 billion cubic meters of water. Wikipedia describes it as one of the largest reservoirs in Southeast Asia. The dam is
high and about
1.6 km

long, irrigates roughly 77,000 hectares of farmland in Central Luzon and generates about 120 megawatts of hydropower. Before it is a sightseeing spot, then, it is a key facility for the rice farming of Nueva Ecija and neighboring provinces.

What makes this lake special is the town beneath it. The dam was authorized in 1966 by Republic Act No. 5499, ground was broken in June 1971, construction was completed in the mid-1970s and the dam is reported to have begun operating in February 1977. In the process, the center of the roughly 300-year-old Old Pantabangan, seven outlying barangays and about 8,100 hectares of farmland were submerged, and residents moved to a new town center built on higher ground. Today's Pantabangan town stands on that resettlement site.

The old town, normally underwater, shows itself during droughts. When El Niño stretches the dry season, the water level falls sharply, and the ruins are recorded as having reappeared in 1983, 2014, 2020, 2024 and 2026. In April 2024 the level dropped more than 50 m below its maximum of about

, a temporary island rose in the middle of the lake, and visitors could see the cross and parts of the walls of the San Andres (St. Andrew) church built in 1825, the cemetery site, the old plaza and the foundations of the municipal hall. The local government has designated the area a cultural heritage zone, and in June 2024 tourism officials were reported to have declared the old townsite a "Heritage Soul."

One thing to keep in mind when planning: the ruins are not a permanent, always-visible attraction. They sink again when the rains return, and how much appears in any given year depends on the drought. On the other hand, even in high-water years you can still enjoy the lake and dam views, the lakeside lookouts and the surrounding mountain ridges, so a trip without ruins is not a wasted one. Before you go, check the current water level and whether the ruins are exposed with the Pantabangan tourism office or local government announcements.

blocks.title: The San Andres church site rising from the water

children.text: The church at the heart of Old Pantabangan is reported to have been built in 1825. When the water drops, the cross and parts of the walls can be seen on the temporary island in the middle of the lake. It was also reported that townspeople held Mass at the exposed church site.

blocks.title: The old cemetery, plaza and municipal hall site

children.text: Besides the church, you can see the cemetery site, the old plaza and the foundations of the municipal hall. One report says that after visiting the church site by boat, visitors had to take a separate boat to reach the cemetery. This was a real town with real residents and graves, so walk through quietly.

blocks.title: A boat ride to the middle of the lake

children.text: You cannot reach the ruins without a boat. Small bangkas operated by local fishermen leave from the dam-side landing. In 2024 reports, one said the boat fare from the dam to the church site was ₱150, while another reported fishermen charging about ₱300. Fares vary with the water level and distance, so confirm on the spot.
The dam viewpoint at Sitio Intang and the lakeside Intang Lake View Deck and Hanging Bridge are separate stops. A
2026 local visitor guide
lists the dam viewpoint as free and the lakeside deck and bridge at
per person. Check access hours and boundaries for the stop you choose.

blocks.title: Emerald water and the Sierra Madre foothills

children.text: Pantabangan lies between the Sierra Madre and Caraballo mountain ranges, at the foot of Mt. Mabilog. When the water is high, the lake looks like a big bay ringed by mountains, a good setting for sunrise and sunset photos.

blocks.title: Forest Garden and lakeside viewpoint walks

children.text: A travel site says the Forest Garden in Pantabangan (Canile Trail) is open daily from 5:00 AM to 5:00 PM and has shaded walking paths, picnic spots and birdwatching. A hiking trail up Mt. Kaanducian with views of the lake is also listed, but confirm fees and the exact route locally.

Pantabangan has held the Pandawan Festival since April 2008. Programs listed include art workshops, a cooking contest, dance competitions and a street parade. The dates can change from year to year, so check local government announcements if you want to time your visit.

The lake has cages for farming tilapia. The Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources is reported to plan an expansion of cage farming for 2023–2028. These are not recreational fishing spots, so keep away from the fish cages.

items.title: Day trip from Manila
items.subtitle: Leave before dawn and see the ruins by boat in the morning

children.text: Head from Manila to a bus terminal for Cabanatuan. Pantabangan is about
from Manila, so an early start is needed.
Arrive in Cabanatuan and transfer to a van or jeepney to Pantabangan. The distance from Cabanatuan to Pantabangan is about
50 km
In Pantabangan, check at the tourism office or the dam landing whether the ruins are open and what the boat fare is. In 2024 the ruins were reported to be open from 6:00 AM to noon.
When the ruins are exposed and boat access is authorized, take a banca from the designated landing. If the site is submerged or sailings are suspended, visit the Intang lakeside viewpoint instead.
Return to town for lunch. In a year when the ruins are closed, enjoy the lake view from the dam area instead.
Go back to Cabanatuan and board a bus to Manila. Allow for traffic on the way back and leave no later than 4:00 PM.
In years when the water is high and no ruins show, boat trips may not run. In that case, build your day around the dam viewpoint, a stroll through town and nearby Minalungao National Park.

items.title: Overnight trip
items.subtitle: The lake and dam, then nearby sights on day two

children.text: Leave Manila, have lunch in Cabanatuan and continue to Pantabangan in the afternoon.
Check in, then walk along the dam to look over the lake. The light is best around sunset.
Have dinner at a restaurant in town. Ask locally whether any freshwater fish dishes from the lake are on offer.
Early on day two, go to the landing in time for the opening hours of the ruins. Before the sun climbs it is cooler and the light on the lake is soft.
If you have time left, stop at nearby Minalungao National Park or Cabanatuan city on your way back.
There are not many places to stay in Pantabangan town, so book ahead or stay in Cabanatuan and travel in. Check exact room rates by date on a booking site.
Take a Five Star bus from Cubao to Cabanatuan Central Terminal. A 2026 listing gives a regular one-way example of
. Confirm the current fare and route at departure.
Pantabangan town is about
from Manila. Travel time varies a lot with traffic, so check schedules and fares at the terminal.
The
Cabanatuan Central Terminal directory
lists the Pantabangan jeepney at
one way. Ask where it stops in relation to the town and dam, and check the last return trip before boarding.
The usual route is via NLEX and the Central Luzon link expressways toward Cabanatuan, then on to Pantabangan. Enter "Pantabangan Dam" in your navigation app.
Part of the road runs through hilly terrain, so plan to arrive before dark.

items.title: Getting around town and on the lake

children.text: Between the town, the dam and the landing you travel by tricycle. Negotiate the fare or confirm it locally.
To reach the ruins you use a fisherman's bangka. Check that life jackets are provided and do not board over capacity.
Bangka fares at the dam landing can change from year to year, so follow local guidance.

The best chance of seeing the old town ruins is in March–May, at the end of the dry season. The 2024 appearance also came in April, together with an El Niño drought. But the ruins sink again when the rains arrive, so whether they are visible when you want to go depends on that year's weather.

If you only want the scenery regardless of the ruins, the cooler months of November–February are also good. The rainy months of June–October bring unstable road and weather conditions, so leave yourself some slack. In April and May the days are very hot with little shade, so bring a hat and water.

rows: The lake is full and the ruins are mostly hidden; good for scenery

There are small lodgings in Pantabangan town, but Cabanatuan city has many more choices. If a day trip is too tiring, a common approach is to stay in Cabanatuan and head out early in the morning. Check room rates and availability by date on a booking site.

Eating in town usually means Filipino home cooking at small restaurants and the market. Whether any tilapia dishes from the lake are served depends on the restaurant, so ask. It is a remote area and many places close early in the evening, so it is safer to have lunch early.
GMA’s July 2026 report
documents parts of the old town resurfacing as the reservoir fell. Ask the tourism office about visibility, landing access and sailings for your date.
The morning hours reported in 2024 applied to the ruins then. Check viewpoint hours and ruins access separately for your date.
At the ruins, do not litter, take away pieces of the structures, cook or camp.
Bring a wide-brimmed hat, sunscreen and water. There is almost no shade on the lake.
Wear a life jacket on the bangka and keep to the passenger limit. Boats may stop running on rough days.
Remember that the old cemetery site is where real residents were buried, and walk through quietly.
Ask fishermen and residents for permission before photographing them.
Combining the trip with Cabanatuan or nearby Minalungao makes for a full day.
Visibility and access to the old town depend on reservoir levels. Confirm that boats are allowed to sail and wear a life jacket before boarding.
Opening hours and the length of your stay at the ruins may be limited, so follow local guidance.
There is no shade in the middle of the lake and April–May is very hot. Watch for dehydration and heatstroke.
In low-water years there are submerged structures and mud, so swimming is not recommended.
Boat fares differed from one report to another, so settle the fare before boarding.
The dam is a facility for irrigation and power, so follow signs and barriers.
A riverside gorge park in General Tinio, also in Nueva Ecija. You can enjoy bamboo rafting and swimming, and it can be combined with a Pantabangan trip. Check current opening status locally.

50 km
